venue.name: Oceanside Community Arts Council
venue.description: The Oceanside Community Arts Council is a non profit registered charity chartered in 1976, covering the area from Nanoose Bay through Parksville and Qualicum Beach to Bowser, the same ground as School District 69. It owns and operates the McMillan Arts Centre in Parksville and keeps its administration office in that building. Its own work is a directory of more than 900 artist and organisation members, a monthly online arts magazine, podcasts and videos, and a short list of local arts events, most of which point at other venues. Nothing on the council's own site is a visit, a class or a session that a school or daycare group can book from the council itself.
venue.hours_notes: The council's office inside the McMillan Arts Centre is open 11 am to 3 pm, Tuesday to Sunday, and closed on statutory holidays. These are office hours rather than hours a group could visit.
venue.seasonal_notes: The council's Oceanside Arts Magazine comes out monthly. Its events list runs on long date ranges rather than a season, with entries stretching from November 2025 to 2029.

gaps: THIS IS THE ORGANISATION BEHIND THE McMILLAN ARTS CENTRE, which is catalogued separately as McMillan Arts Centre - The MAC. The council's own page says it proudly owns and operates the MAC, and its About page says it owns the upper half of the building and runs its operations from there. Anything you would actually book in Parksville, the galleries, the gift shop, the Creative Kids art classes and the MAC School for the Creative Arts, sits on the arts centre's own website and belongs on that record. Both records are kept so that a director who searches for the arts council lands somewhere that tells her where to go, the same way the Nanaimo Arts Council and the Nanaimo Art Gallery are kept apart.

Nothing bookable by a children's group is published on the council's own site. Its pages are a members directory, a magazine, podcasts, videos, a strategic plan, an Elder College link, an Aging Artfully page and a list of local events. There is no field trip, no workshop for a class and no group visit of its own.

The council's events list has a Story Time heading, which sounds promising for young children, but the category is empty. All six live listings are somewhere else or someone else's: two galleries in other buildings, a farmers market in Errington, a regional tourism website, the galleries at the McMillan Arts Centre and the arts school there, and the last two link straight out to the arts centre's site.

The address recorded here is the McMillan Arts Centre building, because that is where the council's office is. Their contact page also gives a post office box. Nothing on the council's site describes washrooms, a place to eat, parking or step free access, because the council does not present itself as somewhere to visit.

No photographs of anything a group would see. The site's images are the council's own logo, a magazine cover, a volunteer wanted line drawing and a poster for a farmers market, so there is no header picture for this record.

Whether the council would put a group in touch with one of its member artists, or arrange a session in a classroom, is not addressed anywhere on the site. It describes itself as a partner of choice for arts organisations and says it wants to develop arts education and outreach for children, but nothing is offered yet.

The council publishes two email addresses, one for exhibitions and classes that goes to the arts centre and one for the artist directory and social network. Neither is a route for booking a group visit, so no email is recorded here. The phone number is the arts centre's front desk.
The site runs on the Ning platform and shows a message asking you to enable JavaScript, but plain fetches returned the full page text and the pages were also opened in a browser to confirm.
